```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Instructor setup, hidden from the page.
# Let PROJ download datum-shift grids from cdn.proj.org. Without them, an
# NAD27 -> NAD83 conversion can silently fall back to a zero shift (see the
# "Behind the scenes" box in section 3). freeze: auto in _quarto.yml saves the
# results, so this only needs the network when the page is re-rendered.
sf::sf_proj_network(TRUE)

# Wider printed output, so data frames don't wrap on the page
options(width = 90)
```

## Why this session

In your homework, two layers that should have overlapped didn't. Something
failed loudly, something failed silently, or both. Today is about *why*, so
that you can spot the problem in any data and in any code an AI writes for you.

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Tell a **geographic** CRS from a **projected** one by reading R's printout.
2. Explain what a **datum** is and when a datum difference matters.
3. Explain why every flat map **distorts** something, and choose a projection
   that protects what your analysis measures.
4. Use **EPSG codes** to name, check, and convert CRSs in R.

---

## 1 The failure, again

We'll use small datasets that come with `terra`: elevation for Luxembourg and
the country's 12 cantons (districts). Both arrive in longitude and latitude.

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| message: false
library(sf)       # vector data
library(terra)    # raster data
library(dplyr)    # filter() and friends
library(spData)   # the `world` dataset, used in section 4
library(units)    # converting m^2 to km^2, used in section 4
```

```{r}
#| label: load
# Elevation raster for Luxembourg
elev_file <- system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
elev <- rast(elev_file)

# The 12 cantons of Luxembourg, as sf polygons
cantons_file <- system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra")
cantons <- st_read(cantons_file)
```

To set up the problem, imagine Luxembourg's mapping agency sends you the
elevation data in their national grid, EPSG:2169. We'll create that version
here. (`project()` converts a raster between CRSs. We'll look at its options
in a later session.)

```{r}
#| label: make-national-grid
elev_lux <- project(elev, "EPSG:2169")
elev_lux
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Predict

Compare the `extent` of `elev_lux` above with the `Bounding box` that
`st_read()` printed for `cantons`. If we draw the cantons on top of the
elevation, what will we see?
:::

```{r}
#| label: overlay-fail
#| fig-height: 5
# Raster first, cantons on top in red
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons), add = TRUE, border = "red")
```

No red lines, no error, no warning. Now two geoprocessing steps:

```{r}
#| label: crop-fail
#| error: true
# Loud failure: crop() checks that the layers overlap, and stops
crop(elev_lux, cantons)
```

```{r}
#| label: extract-fail
# Silent failure: a mean elevation for each canton... all NaN
# (na.rm = TRUE is needed because elev.tif has no-data cells along the border)
bad <- extract(elev_lux, cantons, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
bad
```

Hold on to these three symptoms. The rest of the session explains them, and
in section 6 we fix them.

---

## 2 Geographic vs. projected CRSs

A **coordinate reference system** (CRS) is the set of rules that turns a pair
of numbers into a place on Earth. There are two kinds.

- A **geographic CRS** gives positions as **angles** on a model of the Earth:
  longitude and latitude, in **degrees**. EPSG:4326 (WGS 84) is the most
  common one.
- A **projected CRS** flattens that model onto a plane and gives positions as
  **x and y distances**, usually in **meters** (sometimes feet). Every
  projected CRS is built on top of a geographic one.

The key consequence: **a degree is not a fixed distance.** A degree of
latitude is always about 111 km. A degree of longitude shrinks as you move
toward the poles, because the meridians converge.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Predict

How long is one degree of longitude at Luxembourg's latitude (about 49.6° N)?
More or less than 100 km?
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof lat = Inputs.range([0, 89], {
  value: 38.9, step: 0.1, label: "Latitude (° N)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Length of one degree on a sphere of radius 6,371 km.
// Latitude: constant. Longitude: shrinks with cos(latitude).
kmPerDegLat = 111.2
kmPerDegLon = 111.2 * Math.cos(lat * Math.PI / 180)

// A few reference places, to make the slider concrete
places = [
  {name: "Equator", lat: 0},
  {name: "Washington, DC", lat: 38.9},
  {name: "Luxembourg", lat: 49.6},
  {name: "Oslo", lat: 59.9},
  {name: "Svalbard", lat: 78.2}
]

{
  // Two horizontal bars, drawn to the same scale (111.2 km = full width)
  const w = Math.min(width, 640);
  const bar = (label, km, color) => html`
    <div style="margin:.35rem 0">
      <div style="font-size:.9rem">${label}: <b>${km.toFixed(1)} km</b></div>
      <div style="height:18px;width:${(km / kmPerDegLat) * w}px;background:${color};border-radius:3px"></div>
    </div>`;
  // Buttons that move the slider. Built with DOM calls because Quarto's
  // html`` template doesn't attach functions as event handlers.
  const near = places.map(p => {
    const b = document.createElement("button");
    b.textContent = p.name;
    b.className = "btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary";
    b.style.margin = ".2rem .3rem .2rem 0";
    b.addEventListener("click", () => {
      const input = viewof lat;
      input.value = p.lat;
      input.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
    });
    return b;
  });
  return html`<div class="widget">
    ${bar("1° of latitude", kmPerDegLat, "#7a8ca3")}
    ${bar("1° of longitude", kmPerDegLon, "#d1495b")}
    <div style="margin-top:.5rem;font-size:.9rem">Jump to: ${near}</div>
  </div>`;
}
```

So a "square" one degree on a side is not square on the ground, and its area
depends on where it is. That is why lengths, areas, and buffers measured
directly in degrees are meaningless.

Now read what R tells you. Each object's CRS is in its printout, and there's a
direct yes/no question you can ask:

```{r}
#| label: geographic-check
# Is it longitude/latitude (degrees)?
st_is_longlat(cantons)   # sf objects
is.lonlat(elev_lux)      # terra rasters

# The ranges of the coordinates tell the same story
st_bbox(cantons)
ext(elev_lux)
```

The cantons span about 0.8 degrees east–west. The raster spans about 57,000
meters. Same country, different units, so the numbers don't overlap. That is
the whole story of section 1, and we'll come back to it.

::: {.callout-note}
## A helpful shortcut in sf

When you ask `sf` for an area or distance on longitude/latitude data, it does
the math on the globe and gives you meters (`st_area(cantons)` works). Don't
count on every function being this careful. A raster's cell size, for example,
stays in degrees.
:::

---

## 3 Datums and ellipsoids

Latitude and longitude only mean something once you say **which model of the
Earth** they're measured on.

- The Earth is close to an **ellipsoid**: a sphere squashed at the poles. The
  equatorial radius is about 21 km longer than the polar radius.
- An **ellipsoid** is the mathematical shape (its size and flattening).
- A **datum** is an ellipsoid *plus* how it is pinned to the real Earth: where
  its center is and how it's oriented.

Change the datum and the same coordinates point to a slightly different spot
on the ground.

| Datum | Ellipsoid | Pinned to | Where you'll meet it |
|---|---|---|---|
| NAD27 | Clarke 1866 | A survey point in Kansas (Meades Ranch) | Old maps and surveys |
| NAD83 | GRS 80 | Earth's center (fixed to the North American plate) | US Census / TIGER data, state agencies |
| WGS 84 | WGS 84 | Earth's center (global) | GPS, most web data, EPA TRI |

Let's measure how much a datum matters. Take one set of coordinates for the AU
campus and label it with two datums:

```{r}
#| label: datum-shift
# One pair of numbers: longitude, latitude
au_xy <- st_point(c(-77.0887, 38.9365))

# The same numbers, labeled with two different datums
au_nad27 <- st_sfc(au_xy, crs = 4267)
au_nad83 <- st_sfc(au_xy, crs = 4269)

# Convert the NAD27 point to NAD83, so both are on one datum
au_nad27_converted <- st_transform(au_nad27, 4269)

# How far apart are "the same" coordinates on the ground?
st_distance(au_nad83, au_nad27_converted)
```

About 28 meters, which is enough to put a facility on the wrong side of a
street or a census tract boundary. Between **NAD83 and WGS 84**, the difference
in the US is only about a meter or two. That rarely matters for tract-level
analysis or 30 m rasters.

But R can't know what precision *your* question needs, so it treats any
difference in CRS as a mismatch. That's why, in the asthma problem, the EPA TRI
points (WGS 84) still have to be transformed before they can be joined to the
Census tracts (NAD83).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Behind the scenes: datum shifts need extra files

Accurate NAD27 → NAD83 conversion uses a grid of measured shifts. That grid is
a separate download, not built into R. If PROJ (the library under `sf` and
`terra`) can't find it, it falls back to a "ballpark" conversion. That can
mean **no shift at all, with no error**. This page was built with
`sf_proj_network(TRUE)`, which lets PROJ fetch grids from the internet as
needed. You'll rarely need NAD27 in this course. The lesson is the general
one: a step that runs without error isn't proof that it did what you think.
:::

---

## 4 Projections: flattening is a trade

You can't flatten an orange peel without stretching or tearing it. Map
projections are systematic ways of doing that stretching. They come in
**families**, named after the flat surface the globe is projected onto:

- **Cylindrical**: wrap a cylinder around the globe (Mercator, UTM).
- **Conic**: set a cone on top of it (Albers, Lambert Conformal Conic). Good
  for mid-latitude regions that are wider than they are tall, like the US or
  Maryland.
- **Azimuthal**: touch a flat plane to one point (polar maps, "distance from
  here" maps).

Each projection protects some properties and gives up others:

- **Conformal**: preserves **shape** (angles) locally. Areas get distorted.
- **Equal-area**: preserves **area**. Shapes get distorted.
- **Equidistant**: preserves **distance**, but only from one point or along
  certain lines.
- **Azimuthal**: preserves **direction** from the center point.

**No flat map preserves all of these.** In particular, a map can't be both
conformal and equal-area. So you choose a projection by asking what your
analysis *measures*.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Predict

The red circles below are all the same size on the globe (radius 4°). On the
Mercator map, how will the circles near the poles compare with the circles at
the equator? What about on Equal Earth?
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Data: world countries (Natural Earth via the world-atlas package) ----
tc = require("topojson-client@3.1.0")
worldTopo = FileAttachment("countries-110m.json").json()
land = tc.feature(worldTopo, worldTopo.objects.land)
countries = tc.feature(worldTopo, worldTopo.objects.countries).features

// ---- Shared geometry for the projection explorer ----
// Tissot circles: identical 4-degree circles on a 30 x 15 degree grid
tissot = {
  const circles = [];
  for (let lon = -180; lon < 180; lon += 30) {
    for (let lat = -75; lat <= 75; lat += 15) {
      circles.push(d3.geoCircle().center([lon, lat]).radius(4)());
    }
  }
  return {type: "GeometryCollection", geometries: circles};
}

// The shortest route on the globe (a great circle) from DC to London
route = ({type: "LineString", coordinates: [[-77.04, 38.90], [-0.13, 51.51]]})

// Boxes to fit maps to. Mercator can't show the poles (they're infinitely
// far away), so its world view stops at 60° S and 84° N.
naBox = d3.geoGraticule().extent([[-128, 18], [-62, 56]]).outline()
mercBox = d3.geoGraticule().extent([[-180, -60], [180, 84]]).outline()
fitTarget = view => view === "na" ? naBox : view === "merc" ? mercBox : {type: "Sphere"}

// ---- The projections on offer, with the facts shown in the info card ----
projections = new Map([
  ["Equirectangular (plain lon/lat)", {
    make: () => d3.geoEquirectangular(),
    view: "world", family: "Cylindrical",
    keeps: "Distance along meridians only",
    gives: "Area and shape, badly near the poles",
    epsg: "What you get when you plot EPSG:4326 data as x/y",
    use: "Quick looks. Not for measuring anything."
  }],
  ["Mercator", {
    make: () => d3.geoMercator(),
    view: "merc", family: "Cylindrical",
    keeps: "Shape (conformal); compass directions are straight lines",
    gives: "Area: grows rapidly toward the poles",
    epsg: "3857 (Web Mercator, used by web maps), 3395",
    use: "Navigation, web basemaps. Never for area."
  }],
  ["Equal Earth", {
    make: () => d3.geoEqualEarth(),
    view: "world", family: "Pseudocylindrical",
    keeps: "Area (equal-area)",
    gives: "Shape, especially near the edges",
    epsg: "8857",
    use: "World maps of anything per area: density, rates, land cover."
  }],
  ["Albers Equal Area Conic (US)", {
    make: () => d3.geoConicEqualArea().parallels([29.5, 45.5]).rotate([96, 0]),
    view: "na", family: "Conic",
    keeps: "Area (equal-area)",
    gives: "Shape, slightly, away from the two standard parallels",
    epsg: "5070 (NAD83 / Conus Albers, used by NLCD)",
    use: "Areas and densities across the US."
  }],
  ["Lambert Conformal Conic (Maryland)", {
    make: () => d3.geoConicConformal().parallels([38.3, 39.45]).rotate([77, 0]),
    view: "na", family: "Conic",
    keeps: "Shape (conformal)",
    gives: "Area, growing away from Maryland's latitudes",
    epsg: "26985 (NAD83 / Maryland, meters), 2248 (same, US feet)",
    use: "State Plane: Maryland agency data, local measurement."
  }],
  ["Transverse Mercator (UTM zone 18N)", {
    make: () => d3.geoTransverseMercator().rotate([75, 0]),
    view: "na", family: "Cylindrical (turned sideways)",
    keeps: "Shape (conformal)",
    gives: "Scale grows east and west of the central meridian (75° W)",
    epsg: "26918 (NAD83 / UTM 18N), 32618 (WGS 84 / UTM 18N)",
    use: "Distances and buffers within a 6°-wide zone (DC, MD, VA)."
  }],
  ["Azimuthal Equidistant (centered on DC)", {
    make: () => d3.geoAzimuthalEquidistant().rotate([77.04, -38.9]),
    view: "world", family: "Azimuthal",
    keeps: "Distance and direction from the center point (DC)",
    gives: "Area and shape, worst far from the center",
    epsg: "No standard code; defined around any center you choose",
    use: "\"How far is everything from here?\" maps."
  }],
  ["Orthographic (a view of the globe)", {
    make: () => d3.geoOrthographic().rotate([77.04, -38.9]),
    view: "world", family: "Azimuthal (perspective)",
    keeps: "Looks like the globe from space",
    gives: "Shows only half the Earth; area and distance squeezed at the edge",
    epsg: "Rarely used for analysis",
    use: "Visual reference: compare the other maps with this one."
  }]
])
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof projName = Inputs.select([...projections.keys()], {
  label: "Projection", value: "Mercator"
})
viewof layers = Inputs.checkbox(["Tissot circles", "Route: DC → London"], {
  value: ["Tissot circles", "Route: DC → London"]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const p = projections.get(projName);
  // Map uses the full page width (best when projected in class); the info
  // card sits underneath it
  const w = width;
  const h = Math.round(w * 0.58);

  // Build the projection and fit it to the world, Mercator's box, or North
  // America. clipExtent keeps conic/transverse maps from drawing off-screen.
  const projection = p.make()
    .fitExtent([[8, 8], [w - 8, h - 8]], fitTarget(p.view))
    .clipExtent([[0, 0], [w, h]]);
  const path = d3.geoPath(projection);

  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, w, h]).style("width", "100%");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", "#eef3f7");
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(d3.geoGraticule10()))
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#cfd8e0").attr("stroke-width", 0.5);
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", "#c9c4b8");
  if (layers.includes("Tissot circles")) {
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(tissot))
      .attr("fill", "#d1495b").attr("fill-opacity", 0.55);
  }
  if (layers.includes("Route: DC → London")) {
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(route))
      .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#1f5f8b").attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
  }
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"}))
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#9aa5ad");

  // Each fact is its own <div> so the card can flow into columns
  const card = html`<dl class="proj-card">
    <div><dt>Family</dt><dd>${p.family}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Preserves</dt><dd>${p.keeps}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Gives up</dt><dd>${p.gives}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>EPSG codes</dt><dd>${p.epsg}</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Use it for</dt><dd>${p.use}</dd></div>
  </dl>`;

  return html`<div class="widget">${svg.node()}${card}</div>`;
}
```

Things to try:

- **Mercator vs. Equal Earth:** compare the circles near the poles. Which map
  keeps their *size* and which keeps their *shape*?
- **The DC → London route** is the shortest path on the globe. On which
  projection is it a straight line? (Hint: one of them measures distance from
  DC.)
- **The two conic maps** look almost the same over Maryland. Over that small
  area, the distortion differences are tiny. This is why a sensible local CRS
  matters much more than the "perfect" one.

### How big is Greenland, really?

On Mercator, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. Drag it south and watch
what happens on each map. Its true size never changes. The Democratic
Republic of the Congo (DRC, in blue) stays put for comparison.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof targetLat = Inputs.range([0, 73], {
  value: 73, step: 1, label: "Greenland's center latitude (° N)"
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Move a country along its own meridian to a new center latitude by rotating
// it on the globe. Rotation keeps its true size and shape.
function moveTo(feature, newLat) {
  const [lon0, lat0] = d3.geoCentroid(feature);
  const toOrigin = d3.geoRotation([-lon0, -lat0]);   // centroid -> (0, 0)
  const toTarget = d3.geoRotation([-lon0, -newLat]); // (lon0, newLat) -> (0, 0)
  const move = pt => toTarget.invert(toOrigin(pt));
  const walk = c => typeof c[0] === "number" ? move(c) : c.map(walk);
  return {type: "Feature", geometry: {
    type: feature.geometry.type, coordinates: walk(feature.geometry.coordinates)
  }};
}

greenland = countries.find(d => d.properties.name === "Greenland")
drc = countries.find(d => d.properties.name === "Dem. Rep. Congo")
movedGreenland = moveTo(greenland, targetLat)

{
  const wide = width > 700;
  const w = wide ? Math.floor((width - 40) / 2) : width;
  const h = Math.round(w * 0.75);

  // Draw one panel and report Greenland's apparent size relative to the DRC
  function panel(title, makeProjection, view) {
    const projection = makeProjection().fitExtent([[6, 6], [w - 6, h - 6]], fitTarget(view));
    const path = d3.geoPath(projection);
    const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, w, h]).style("width", "100%");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path({type: "Sphere"})).attr("fill", "#eef3f7");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(land)).attr("fill", "#dcd8cf");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(greenland))
      .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#d1495b").attr("stroke-dasharray", "3 3");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(drc)).attr("fill", "#1f5f8b");
    svg.append("path").attr("d", path(movedGreenland)).attr("fill", "#d1495b");
    const looks = path.area(movedGreenland) / path.area(drc);
    return html`<div>
      <div style="font-weight:600">${title}</div>${svg.node()}
      <div>Greenland looks <span class="readout">${looks.toFixed(1)}×</span> the DRC</div>
    </div>`;
  }

  // True ratio, measured on the globe
  const truth = d3.geoArea(greenland) / d3.geoArea(drc);

  return html`<div class="widget">
    <div style="display:${wide ? "grid" : "block"};grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:1rem">
      ${panel("Mercator (conformal)", d3.geoMercator, "merc")}
      ${panel("Equal Earth (equal-area)", d3.geoEqualEarth, "world")}
    </div>
    <p style="margin:.75rem 0 0">On the globe, Greenland is
      <b>${truth.toFixed(2)}×</b> the size of the DRC, wherever you put it.
      The dashed outline is where Greenland actually is.</p>
  </div>`;
}
```

The same comparison in R, using the `world` dataset from the `spData`
package:

```{r}
#| label: areas
# `world` (from spData) is in EPSG:4326
two <- filter(world, name_long %in% c("Greenland", "Democratic Republic of the Congo"))

# The same two countries in two projected CRSs
two_merc <- st_transform(two, 3857)   # Web Mercator
two_ee   <- st_transform(two, 8857)   # Equal Earth

# Area on the globe (sf does this for lon/lat data), then on each flat map
area_globe <- st_area(two)
area_merc  <- st_area(two_merc)
area_ee    <- st_area(two_ee)

# Convert from square meters to square kilometers
area_globe <- set_units(area_globe, km^2)
area_merc  <- set_units(area_merc, km^2)
area_ee    <- set_units(area_ee, km^2)

data.frame(country = two$name_long, area_globe, area_merc, area_ee)
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Discuss

Each number above was computed correctly. Which one would you report as
Greenland's area, and why? Which one would an AI report if it "helpfully"
transformed your data to 3857 first?
:::

## 5 EPSG codes: names for CRSs

Saying "NAD83, Lambert Conformal Conic, standard parallels 38.3° and 39.45°,
meters" every time would be painful. The **EPSG registry** (now maintained by
IOGP, the oil and gas producers' association) gives each complete CRS
definition a number. One code bundles the datum, the ellipsoid, the
projection and its parameters, and the units.

Codes you'll meet in this course:

| EPSG | Name | Type | Units | Where you'll see it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4326 | WGS 84 | Geographic | degrees | GPS, most web data, EPA TRI |
| 4269 | NAD83 | Geographic | degrees | Census tracts via `tidycensus` |
| 4267 | NAD27 | Geographic | degrees | Old maps and surveys |
| 3857 | WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator | Projected, cylindrical | "meters" (stretched) | Web map tiles. Display only. |
| 5070 | NAD83 / Conus Albers | Projected, conic, equal-area | meters | NLCD; areas across the US |
| 26918 | NAD83 / UTM zone 18N | Projected, transverse Mercator | meters | Distances in DC, MD, VA |
| 26985 | NAD83 / Maryland | Projected, Lambert conic | meters | Maryland state data |
| 2248 | NAD83 / Maryland (ftUS) | Projected, Lambert conic | **US feet** | Maryland county GIS. Check the units! |

You don't need to memorize these. You need to know how to **read** one. Ask
`terra` for a short description, or print the full definition with `sf`:

```{r}
#| label: read-epsg
# Short summary: name, code, and where it's meant to be used
crs("EPSG:26985", describe = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-wkt
# The full definition (called WKT). Skim for these four things:
#   the name on the first line (PROJCRS = projected; GEOGCRS = geographic)
#   DATUM and ELLIPSOID
#   METHOD (the projection)
#   LENGTHUNIT under AXIS (the units of x and y)
st_crs(26985)
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Choose a CRS

For each task, pick a CRS from the table and defend it in one sentence.

1. Total impervious area in each Maryland county.
2. Number of TRI facilities within 1 km of each census tract centroid in
   Baltimore.
3. Asthma prevalence compared across all 48 contiguous states.
4. An interactive web map for a community group.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Some defensible answers

1. **5070** (equal-area) or **26985**. Within one state, State Plane's area
   distortion is tiny, so either is defensible. Saying *why* is the point.
2. **26985** or **26918**: both are in meters and accurate locally for
   distance. Not 4326: a 1 km buffer needs meters.
3. **5070**: equal-area across the whole country.
4. **3857** for *display*. Do the analysis in a measuring CRS first, then
   transform for the map.
:::

---

## 6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it

Now the symptoms from section 1 make sense:

- The cantons' coordinates are around **6 and 50** (degrees). The raster's are
  in the **tens of thousands** (meters).
- `plot()` just draws numbers. It put the cantons in a tiny patch near
  x = 6, y = 50, far outside the raster's extent, so nothing appeared on the
  map.
- `crop()` compared the two extents, found no overlap, and **stopped**.
- `extract()` found no raster cells inside any polygon and returned `NaN`,
  **without complaint**.

The fix is to put both layers in one CRS. Transform the **vector** to match
the raster, not the other way around. Moving polygon vertices is exact, while
reprojecting a raster has to resample cell values.

```{r}
#| label: fix
# Convert the cantons into the raster's CRS
cantons_lux <- st_transform(cantons, crs(elev_lux))

# Check 1: do the two CRSs now match?
st_crs(cantons_lux) == st_crs(elev_lux)

# Check 2: are the coordinate ranges now comparable?
st_bbox(cantons_lux)
ext(elev_lux)
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-plot
#| fig-height: 5
# Check 3: look at it
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons_lux), add = TRUE, border = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-extract
# The zonal mean now works: one number per canton
good <- extract(elev_lux, cantons_lux, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
cantons_lux$elev_mean <- good$elevation

# Check 4: no missing values, and plausible elevations (meters)
sum(is.na(cantons_lux$elev_mean))
summary(cantons_lux$elev_mean)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Labeling is not converting

`st_transform()` **converts** coordinates: the numbers change. `st_set_crs()`
(or `st_crs(x) <- ...`) only **relabels** them: the numbers stay the same.
Relabeling is correct only when a file has *no* CRS and you know what it
should be. AI assistants sometimes suggest it as a "fix" for a mismatch.
Here's what that does:

```{r}
#| label: relabel-trap
# Wrong: claims the degrees are now meters
cantons_relabeled <- st_set_crs(cantons, 2169)
st_bbox(cantons_relabeled)
```

R warns you, and the bounding box gives it away: the "meters" are still 5.7
to 50.2. In EPSG:2169, coordinates that small sit at the grid's origin, which
is in France, about 120 km southwest of Luxembourg's center.
:::

---

## 7 In your code

| Question | Function | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| What CRS is this? | Print the object; `st_crs(x)`; `crs(r, describe = TRUE)` | Name, EPSG code, units |
| Degrees or meters? | `st_is_longlat(x)`; `is.lonlat(r)` | `TRUE` means degrees |
| Do my layers match? | `st_crs(a) == st_crs(b)`; compare `st_bbox()` and `ext()` | Same CRS; ranges that overlap |
| Does it look right? | `plot()` the raster, then the vector with `add = TRUE` | Lines where you expect them |
| Convert a vector | `st_transform(x, crs)` | The bbox numbers change |
| Convert a raster | `project(r, crs)` | Resamples values (later session) |
| Label a CRS-less file | `st_set_crs(x, crs)` | Only when the CRS is missing *and* known |

The habit that ties it together: **check the CRS before any operation that
combines two layers**, and check the result after. Most CRS mistakes don't
produce errors. They produce wrong answers.

## 8 Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A bounding box reads `xmin: 316268 ymin: 4295630 xmax: 334407 ymax: 4318264`. Degrees or meters? Projected or geographic?

Meters, so it's projected. Longitudes only go to ±180 and latitudes to ±90.
Numbers in the hundreds of thousands and millions look like UTM. (This is
Washington, DC, in UTM zone 18N.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why did `extract()` return `NaN` instead of an error?

It did what it was asked: it looked for raster cells inside each polygon and
found none, because the polygons sat far outside the raster's extent. An empty
result isn't an error to the function. Only you know it's wrong, which is why
you check for NAs after every extract.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. An AI's code calls `st_transform(tracts, 3857)` before computing `st_area()`. What's the problem?

Web Mercator inflates area by a factor that grows with latitude. At Maryland's
latitude (about 39° N), that's about 1.66×, so every area would be about
two-thirds too large. Use 5070 or 26985, or compute the area on the original lon/lat
data.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. TRI facilities are in EPSG:4326 and tracts are in EPSG:4269. The difference is about a meter. Why transform anyway?

Because `sf` requires both layers to have the *same* CRS before it will join
them, and it can't judge whether a meter matters for your question. Transform
one to match the other (or both to a projected CRS you'll measure in) and the
join runs.
:::
